title: Descending control: the brain talks back
objective: Explain how descending modulation changes how much pain is felt.

steps.title: Pain is not a fixed readout
steps.body: The brain sends signals *down* to the dorsal horn — **[[descending modulation]]** from regions like the **[[periaqueductal gray]] (PAG)** — that can suppress or amplify incoming pain. The same injury can hurt more or less depending on this top-down state.

steps.setup: A soldier is wounded mid-battle but reports feeling little pain until later.
options: Descending modulation is suppressing pain transmission at the time
Nociceptors at the wound adapt quickly and stop firing
Pain signals travel far too slowly to arrive during the battle
Adrenaline physically blocks conduction in the spinal cord
steps.reveal: Strong top-down (descending) inhibition can clamp pain transmission in the dorsal horn during intense states, so the signal is dampened before it's ever felt — then returns when that state fades.

variants.prompt: Feeling little pain from a serious wound during a crisis reflects…
options: Nociceptors at the wound adapting and going silent
Pain signals being too slow to arrive
variants.explanation: Top-down modulation suppresses the signal at the dorsal horn during the crisis.

steps.prompt: Descending modulation can do which of the following?
options: Either dampen or amplify incoming pain, depending on state
Only dampen incoming pain; it has no way to amplify it
Only amplify incoming pain; it has no way to dampen it
Silence the nociceptor endings out in the skin itself
steps.explanation: The descending system is bidirectional: it can inhibit pain (stress-induced analgesia) or facilitate it (contributing to chronic pain). It modulates, it doesn't delete.

variants.setup: The descending pain-control system is engaged.
variants.prompt: What can it do to incoming pain?
options: Turn it down or up, depending on state
Only ever turn the pain up, never down
Only ever turn the pain down, never up
variants.reveal: It's bidirectional — inhibiting or facilitating pain depending on the brain's state.
